questions.prompt: In the zombie argument against physicalism, a philosophical zombie is...

options.text: a being physically identical to a conscious human, but with no conscious experience at all
a person in a persistent vegetative state
options.why_wrong: Such a patient differs physically and behaviorally from a typical conscious person.

options.text: a robot that behaves like a human but is built from different parts
options.why_wrong: A zombie is a physical duplicate, not merely a behavioral one.

options.text: a person who acts out of habit without thinking
options.why_wrong: Zombies lack experience entirely, not just reflection.

questions.explanation: Chalmers argues that zombies are conceivable and therefore possible, and that if they are possible, facts about consciousness are not fixed by the physical facts.

sources.citation: Chalmers, D. J. (1996). The Conscious Mind: In Search of a Fundamental Theory. Oxford University Press.
Kirk, R. Zombies. In E. N. Zalta (Ed.), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

questions.prompt: The zombie argument and the knowledge argument both target physicalism. How do they mainly differ?

options.text: The zombie argument appeals to what is conceivable; the knowledge argument appeals to what can be learned
The zombie argument is about memory; the knowledge argument is about free will
Only the knowledge argument is about consciousness
options.why_wrong: Both concern conscious experience and its relation to the physical.

options.text: Only the zombie argument was offered against physicalism
options.why_wrong: Jackson originally offered the knowledge argument against physicalism too.

questions.explanation: The zombie argument moves from the conceivability of a physical duplicate without experience to its possibility. The knowledge argument moves from Mary learning something new to the existence of non-physical facts.

sources.citation: Chalmers, D. J. (1996). The Conscious Mind: In Search of a Fundamental Theory. Oxford University Press.
Jackson, F. (1982). Epiphenomenal qualia. The Philosophical Quarterly, 32(127), 127-136.

questions.prompt: Match each thought experiment to the philosopher best known for it.

pairs.left: What is it like to be a bat?

questions.explanation: Each thought experiment is associated with the philosopher who made it famous. Chalmers popularized the zombie argument; the term was used earlier by Robert Kirk.

sources.citation: Jackson, F. (1982). Epiphenomenal qualia. The Philosophical Quarterly, 32(127), 127-136.
Nagel, T. (1974). What is it like to be a bat? The Philosophical Review, 83(4), 435-450.
Searle, J. R. (1980). Minds, brains, and programs. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 3(3), 417-457.
Chalmers, D. J. (1996). The Conscious Mind: In Search of a Fundamental Theory. Oxford University Press.
Kirk, R. Zombies. In E. N. Zalta (Ed.), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

questions.answer_text: A being physically and functionally identical to a conscious human, atom for atom, but with no experience at all.
questions.explanation: A zombie behaves exactly as you do, including talking about its experiences, yet there is nothing it is like to be it. Chalmers argues that if such a being is conceivable, consciousness is not fixed by the physical facts.

sources.citation: Chalmers, D. J. (1996). The Conscious Mind: In Search of a Fundamental Theory. Oxford University Press.

questions.prompt: The zombie argument runs: (1) a zombie world is conceivable; (2) if conceivable, it is metaphysically possible; (3) if possible, consciousness is not fixed by the physical; (4) so physicalism is false. Which step do Type-B physicalists deny?

options.text: Step 1: zombies are not really conceivable
options.why_wrong: Denying conceivability is the Type-A response.

options.text: Step 2: conceivability does not entail metaphysical possibility
Step 3: possibility of zombies is compatible with physicalism
options.why_wrong: Almost no one denies step 3; it is close to a definition of physicalism.

options.text: None: they accept the conclusion

questions.explanation: Type-B physicalists grant that zombies seem conceivable but deny that this shows they are possible, because phenomenal and physical concepts can co-refer without any a priori link. Type-A physicalists instead deny step 1, and illusionists question what the zombie world is supposed to lack.

sources.citation: Chalmers, D. J. (1996). The Conscious Mind: In Search of a Fundamental Theory. Oxford University Press.
Chalmers, D. J. (2003). Consciousness and its place in nature. In S. Stich and T. Warfield (eds.), The Blackwell Guide to Philosophy of Mind. Oxford: Blackwell.

questions.prompt: Why is the inverted spectrum taken to threaten functionalism?

options.text: It shows that colour perception varies across cultures
options.why_wrong: The scenario is about undetectable differences in experience, not cultural variation.

options.text: It shows that colour terms are learned behaviourally
It suggests two people could differ in experience with no functional difference
It shows that colour experience has no neural correlate
options.why_wrong: The scenario makes no claim about neural correlates.

questions.explanation: If your red is my green, systematically, with all discriminations and behaviour matched, then functional role would not fix experience. Locke described the possibility in 1689; functionalists reply that a fully specified inversion may be incoherent or detectable.

sources.citation: Locke, J. (1689). An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, Chapter xxxii, §15. London: Thomas Basset.
Shoemaker, S. (1982). The inverted spectrum. The Journal of Philosophy 79(7), 357-381.

questions.prompt: In the 2020 PhilPapers Survey, which view of zombies was most common among philosophers?

options.text: Zombies are conceivable but not metaphysically possible
Zombies are metaphysically possible
options.why_wrong: This was a minority view, at about a quarter of respondents.

options.text: Zombies are inconceivable
options.why_wrong: This was less common than 'conceivable but not possible'.

options.text: The question is meaningless
options.why_wrong: This was not the most common answer.

questions.explanation: In the 2020 survey about 37 per cent judged zombies conceivable but not metaphysically possible, against about 24 per cent who judged them metaphysically possible. The majority thus rejects the move from conceivability to possibility, the Type-B line. These are 2020 figures and may shift in later surveys.

sources.citation: Bourget, D. and Chalmers, D. J. (2023). Philosophers on philosophy: the 2020 PhilPapers survey. Philosophers' Imprint 23, 11.
